title: Dictionaries and sets
summary: Look values up by key with Dictionary, and keep a collection free of duplicates with HashSet.

steps.title: Looking things up by key
body: A list finds items by position: item 0, item 1. Often you want to find them by something meaningful instead: the price *of an apple*, the age *of Sam*.
A **`Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`** stores **pairs**. You hand it a key and it hands back the value stored under it.
prices["apple"] = 35;              // same key: the value is replaced
- The two types in the angle brackets are the key type and the value type. Here: string keys, int values.
- `dict[key] = value` adds the pair, or **replaces** the value if the key is already there.
- Each key appears only once. Values may repeat.
Looking up a key is fast no matter how many pairs there are. The dictionary does not search from the start the way `List.Contains` does.

steps.explain: The fourth line reads the 3 stored under `apple`, adds 4 and stores 7 back under the same key. No new pair is created, so there are still two.

steps.title: When the key is not there
body: Reading a key that does not exist crashes the program with a **KeyNotFoundException**.
So ask first. `ContainsKey` answers yes or no:
That looks the key up twice. `TryGetValue` does the asking and the fetching in one step. It is the *Try* pattern with an `out` parameter that you know from `int.TryParse`:

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Sam's age when it is known, and `Unknown` when it is not.
steps.explain: `TryGetValue` returns `true` and fills in `age` when the key exists. `ContainsKey` takes only the key, so it cannot be the one with two arguments.

steps.title: Help for any alias
prompt: Sidekick understands aliases: your `Sk.ResolveCommand(word)` from Control flow turns `"t"`, `"Today"` or `""` into `"today"`, and returns any unknown word lowercased. It is ready to call.
Write `static string HelpFor(string word, Dictionary<string, string> help)`. Resolve the word, then look the command up in `help`:
- not found: return `"No help for <word>"` (the word as typed).
With `help` = `{ "today": "your day", "add": "add a task" }`: `HelpFor("t", help)` returns `"today: your day"`, `HelpFor("dance", help)` returns `"No help for dance"`.
starter: static string HelpFor(string word, Dictionary<string, string> help)
solution: static string HelpFor(string word, Dictionary<string, string> help)
template: var dojoHelp = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["today"] = "your day", ["add"] = "add a task", ["week"] = "your week" };
Dojo.Eq("t means today", "today: your day", HelpFor("t", dojoHelp));
Dojo.Eq("an alias in capitals", "add: add a task", HelpFor("NEW", dojoHelp));
Dojo.Eq("the full name works too", "week: your week", HelpFor("week", dojoHelp));
Dojo.Eq("a known command without help", "No help for done", HelpFor("done", dojoHelp));
Dojo.Eq("an unknown word", "No help for dance", HelpFor("dance", dojoHelp));
hints: `help.TryGetValue(command, out string? text)` is `true` when the key exists and puts its value in `text`.

steps.title: Visiting every pair, and counting
body: `foreach` over a dictionary gives you one **pair** per pass. Each pair has a `Key` and a `Value`.
`prices.Keys` and `prices.Values` give you just one side, if that is all you need.
The most common job for a dictionary is **counting things**. The key is the thing, the value is how many you have seen:
First sighting: store 1. Every sighting after that: add 1. The `if` is needed because `counts[c]++` has to *read* the old value, and reading a missing key crashes.
> **Tip:** do not rely on the order in which a dictionary hands out its pairs. If order matters, keep the keys in a list as well, or sort them.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program counts each letter of `"hello"` and prints how many times `l` appears.
steps.explain: A key that is already there gets one more. A new key starts at 1. Swap those two lines and the very first letter crashes, because `counts[c]++` would read a key that does not exist yet.

steps.title: HashSet: no duplicates, fast lookups
body: Sometimes you do not need values at all. You only need to know **whether you have seen something before**. That is a **`HashSet<T>`**: a collection where every item appears at most once.
Console.WriteLine(seen.Add("cat"));   // False: already there, nothing changes
- `Add` returns a `bool` telling you whether the item was actually added. Adding a duplicate is not an error. It is simply ignored.
- `Contains` is as fast as a dictionary lookup, however large the set.
A set has no positions, so there is no `seen[0]`. You can still `foreach` over it.

steps.explain: The second `Add(4)` finds 4 already in the set, returns `false` and changes nothing. The set holds 4 and 7.

steps.prompt: Which collection fits each job best?
items: The moves of a game, in the order they were played
Look up a phone number by name
How many times each word appears in a text
The different tags used across all posts, each once

steps.title: Election night
prompt: The votes are in, as an array of names. Write three methods.
- `Dictionary<string, int> Tally(string[] votes)` returns how many votes each name received.
- `string Winner(Dictionary<string, int> tally)` returns the name with the most votes. You may assume there is at least one name and no tie for first place.
- `int DistinctCount(string[] votes)` returns how many **different** names were voted for. Use a `HashSet`.
For the votes `tea, coffee, tea, juice, tea, coffee`: the tally is tea 3, coffee 2, juice 1; the winner is `tea`; the distinct count is `3`.
starter: // find the key with the highest value
// add every vote, then ask the set how big it is
template: Dojo.Eq("Tally counts 3 votes for tea", 3, dojoTally.GetValueOrDefault("tea"));
Dojo.Eq("Tally counts 2 votes for coffee", 2, dojoTally.GetValueOrDefault("coffee"));
Dojo.Eq("Tally counts 1 vote for juice", 1, dojoTally.GetValueOrDefault("juice"));
Dojo.Eq("Tally of no votes is empty", 0, Tally(new string[0]).Count);
Dojo.Eq("Winner of tea 3, coffee 2, juice 1 is tea", "tea", Winner(new Dictionary<string, int> { ["tea"] = 3, ["coffee"] = 2, ["juice"] = 1 }));
Dojo.Eq("Winner of a 1, b 5, c 2 is b", "b", Winner(new Dictionary<string, int> { ["a"] = 1, ["b"] = 5, ["c"] = 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("Winner of x 1, y 2, z 9 is z", "z", Winner(new Dictionary<string, int> { ["x"] = 1, ["y"] = 2, ["z"] = 9 }));
Dojo.Eq("DistinctCount of the six votes is 3", 3, DistinctCount(dojoVotes));
Dojo.Eq("DistinctCount of { a, a, a } is 1", 1, DistinctCount(new[] { "a", "a", "a" }));
Dojo.Eq("DistinctCount of no votes is 0", 0, DistinctCount(new string[0]));
hints: `Tally` is the counting pattern: for each vote, if the key is already there add 1, otherwise store 1.
`Winner` is the "best so far" pattern. Keep a `best` name and a `bestCount`, loop with `foreach (var pair in tally)`, and update both when `pair.Value > bestCount`.
`DistinctCount`: `Add` every vote to a `HashSet<string>` and return its `Count`. The set throws the duplicates away for you.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: the tag tally
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk note` and `sk tags` count your tags. Write three methods.

**1.** `static Dictionary<string, int> TallyTags(IEnumerable<string> tags)` counts how often each tag appears. Tags are trimmed and lowercased first (`" Auth "` and `"auth"` are the same tag); empty tags are skipped. (`IEnumerable<string>` accepts an array, a list, anything you can `foreach` over.)

**2.** `static string TopTag(Dictionary<string, int> tally)` returns the tag with the highest count. On a tie, the one that comes first alphabetically (`string.CompareOrdinal(a, b) < 0` means `a` sorts first). An empty tally gives `""`.
**3.** `static SortedSet<string> SharedTags(IEnumerable<string> lastWeek, IEnumerable<string> thisWeek)` returns the tags used in **both** weeks, trimmed and lowercased, sorted.
starter: static SortedSet<string> SharedTags(IEnumerable<string> lastWeek, IEnumerable<string> thisWeek)
solution: static SortedSet<string> SharedTags(IEnumerable<string> lastWeek, IEnumerable<string> thisWeek)
template: Dojo.Eq("auth counted twice, case and spaces ignored", 2, dojoTally.GetValueOrDefault("auth"));
Dojo.Eq("the empty tag is skipped", false, dojoTally.ContainsKey(""));
Dojo.Eq("a tie goes to the alphabetically first tag", "auth", TopTag(dojoTally));
Dojo.Eq("the clear winner", "ui", TopTag(new Dictionary<string, int> { ["auth"] = 1, ["ui"] = 3, ["db"] = 2 }));
Dojo.Eq("an empty tally has no top tag", "", TopTag(new Dictionary<string, int>()));
Dojo.Eq("tags used both weeks", "auth,ui", string.Join(",", SharedTags(new[] { "auth", "UI", "db" }, new[] { "ui", "Auth", "api" })));
Dojo.Eq("no tags in common", 0, SharedTags(new[] { "a" }, new[] { "b" }).Count);
Dojo.Eq("a list works as well as an array", 1, TallyTags(new List<string> { "x", "X" }).Count);
hints: `TallyTags`: `string tag = raw.Trim().ToLower();`, skip empty ones, then `tally[tag] = tally.GetValueOrDefault(tag) + 1;`.
`TopTag`: keep `best` and `bestCount`; replace them when `count > bestCount`, or when the counts are equal and `string.CompareOrdinal(tag, best) < 0`.
`SharedTags`: put last week's cleaned tags in a `HashSet<string>`, then add each cleaned tag of this week that the set `Contains` to a `SortedSet<string>`.
steps.explain: Three collections, three jobs: the dictionary counts, the `HashSet` answers *have I seen this?* in one step, and the `SortedSet` keeps its items unique and in order.
